title: Reading legacy date fields

blocks.text: A legacy `java.util.Date` reports its year as years since 1900 (`getYear()` is `124` for 2024), and both `Date.getMonth()` and `Calendar.MONTH` count months from 0 (January is `0`, December is `11`). A lenient `Calendar` also accepts impossible values and silently rolls them over: month index `12` becomes January of the next year, and February 30 becomes early March.
You receive such legacy fields from an old system. Write `LegacyFields`:

items: `static LocalDate fromLegacy(int yearsSince1900, int zeroBasedMonth, int dayOfMonth)` returns the calendar date the fields name.
`static int[] toLegacy(LocalDate date)` returns the three legacy fields `{yearsSince1900, zeroBasedMonth, dayOfMonth}` for `date`.

blocks.text: Fields that name no real date are an error, not a date to guess at: `fromLegacy` **throws** `java.time.DateTimeException` for them and never rolls them over the way a lenient `Calendar` does.

cases.says: Legacy fields (years since 1900, a 0-based month, a day) become the right LocalDate, and back.
Month index 12 is refused with a DateTimeException instead of rolling over into January of the next year.
February 30 is refused with a DateTimeException instead of rolling over into March.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: A lenient Calendar rolls impossible fields such as February 30 or month 12 over into another date, where java.time throws a DateTimeException.
Date.getYear() counts years since 1900, so 2024 is 124 and 1900 must be added back.
Calendar and Date count months from 0, so month index 2 is March, while java.time counts from 1.
